subject: frontend
subtopic: Deep links on a static host
question: If a user opens https://shop.example.com/orders/42 directly (or refreshes on that page), do they see the order page?
ai_claim: Yes. The router has a route for /orders/:id, so it renders the Order component for /orders/42.

ai_solution.text: The router defines /orders/:id.
The user requests /orders/42.
The router matches the URL and renders <Order />.
So the order page appears.

failure.misconception: Forgetting the server handles the first request
failure.explanation: On a direct visit or refresh, the browser asks the server for /orders/42. The router runs only after index.html and the JavaScript have loaded, but a plain static server has no file at /orders/42 and returns 404. Navigating inside the app works because the router intercepts those links. Configure the host to serve index.html for unknown paths (an SPA fallback or rewrite).
failure.why_convincing: Clicking through the app from the home page works perfectly, which is how most manual testing is done.

canonical_solution: The static server returns 404 before the router ever runs. Add an SPA fallback so every unknown path serves index.html.

valid_evidence.summary: Open /orders/42 in a new tab: the server responds 404 Not Found.
Configure the host: rewrite /* to /index.html (e.g. Netlify _redirects: '/*  /index.html  200').

counterexamples: Refreshing any page other than / shows the server's 404 page.

hints.text: Ask who handles the very first request for /orders/42.
Step 3 assumes the router is already running.
Client-side routing starts only after the server has returned index.html.
Refresh the browser while on /orders/42.
Step 3 is wrong: the server looks for a file at /orders/42 and returns 404. Add an SPA fallback to index.html.

repair: Add a rewrite from all unknown paths to /index.html on the host.
debrief: Client-side routes are invisible to the server. Every SPA deployment needs a fallback rule, and the only reliable test is loading a deep URL directly, not clicking to it.

subject: frontend
question: After adding three items and clicking the Cart link, does the cart page still show three items?
ai_claim: Yes. The app is a single-page app, so moving to /cart keeps all in-memory state, including the cart.

ai_solution.text: The cart is stored in React context.
The app is a single-page application.
Following a link in an SPA does not reload the page.
So the cart still has three items.

failure.misconception: Assuming every link in an SPA is a client-side navigation
failure.explanation: A plain <a href> makes the browser perform a full page load. The whole app restarts, React context is recreated empty, and the cart shows zero items. Client-side navigation needs the router's <Link to="/cart"> (or navigate()), which updates the URL without reloading.
failure.why_convincing: The app is an SPA, and <Link> renders an <a> element too, so the two look interchangeable.

canonical_solution: No: <a href> triggers a full reload, wiping in-memory state. Use <Link to="/cart">.

valid_evidence.summary: Click the link with DevTools open: a full document request for /cart is made and the cart is empty.

counterexamples: The cart count drops to 0 after clicking the link.

hints.text: Check what kind of navigation a plain anchor performs.
Step 3 assumes all links in an SPA avoid reloading.
Only the router's Link component intercepts clicks; a plain anchor loads a new document.
Watch the network panel as you click the link.
Step 3 is wrong: <a href> reloads the page and resets in-memory state. Use <Link>.

repair: Replace the anchor with the router's `<Link to="/cart">`.
debrief: Being an SPA is a property of how navigation is done, not of the app as a whole. One plain anchor quietly reloads everything. In-memory state is also lost on refresh, so persist anything users would miss.

subject: frontend
question: When the parent passes an updated products list (a new product arrives), does the visible list include it?
ai_claim: Yes. visible is computed from products whenever the user searches, so it always reflects the current products.

ai_solution.text: visible starts as the full products list.
Each search recomputes visible from products.
So visible is always derived from products.
A new product therefore appears in the list.

failure.misconception: Recomputing derived state on only one of its inputs
failure.explanation: visible depends on both query and products, but it is recomputed only when the user searches. useState(products) uses the initial prop only once, so a new products prop leaves visible unchanged until the next keystroke. Derive it during render instead: const visible = products.filter(p => p.name.includes(query)).
failure.why_convincing: The search path works, and in a demo products rarely change while the page is open.

canonical_solution: No: visible is updated only on search, so new products are missing until the user types. Compute visible during render (useMemo if expensive).

valid_evidence.summary: Render with 3 products, then pass 4 without typing: only 3 are shown.
const visible = useMemo(() => products.filter(p => p.name.includes(query)), [products, query]);

counterexamples: A product added by the parent never appears until the user searches again.

hints.text: List every input that visible depends on.
Step 3 claims visible is always derived from products.
Derived values stored in state go stale when any input changes outside the update path.
Change the products prop without typing.
Step 3 is wrong: visible updates only on search, so new products are missed. Derive it during render.

repair: Remove the visible state; compute it from products and query while rendering.
debrief: Storing derived data in state creates two sources of truth that must be kept in sync by hand. If a value can be computed from props and state, compute it - and memoise if needed.

subject: frontend
question: On /orders/42, is order 42 displayed?
ai_claim: Yes. useParams gives id = 42 from the URL, and find returns the order whose id is 42.

ai_solution.text: The route /orders/:id matches /orders/42.
useParams returns id as 42.
orders.find compares each order's id with 42 using ===.
Order 42 matches and is displayed.

failure.misconception: Assuming URL parameters keep their numeric type
failure.explanation: Everything in a URL is text, so useParams returns id as the string '42'. The order ids are numbers, and 42 === '42' is false, so find returns undefined and the page says 'Order not found'. Convert the parameter: Number(id).
failure.why_convincing: Printed on screen, 42 and '42' look identical.

canonical_solution: useParams returns '42' (a string), so the strict comparison with the number 42 fails. Compare with Number(id).

valid_evidence.summary: '42' === 42 is false, so find returns undefined and 'Order not found' is shown.

counterexamples: Every order page shows 'Order not found'.

hints.text: Check the type of values that come from a URL.
Step 2 states the value of id without its type.
Route parameters and query strings are always strings.
Evaluate '42' === 42.
Step 2 is wrong: id is the string '42', so === fails. Convert with Number(id).

repair: Convert the parameter with `Number(id)` (and handle NaN).
debrief: URLs carry strings. Any value read from a route parameter, query string or form field needs explicit conversion before being compared with typed data.

subject: frontend
question: Is it correct that storing the filter in the URL means a refreshed page, a shared link and the Back button all show the matching filter?
ai_claim: Yes. The filter lives in the query string, so refreshing or sharing the URL restores it, and each change adds a history entry that Back returns to.

ai_solution.text: Selecting a category calls setParams, which updates the URL, e.g. ?category=lamps.
On load, category is read from the URL, so a refresh or shared link restores it.
setParams pushes a new history entry by default.
Pressing Back restores the previous URL and therefore the previous filter.

canonical_solution: Correct. With the URL as the source of truth for the filter, the view is reproducible from the link, and history navigation works for free. (Pass { replace: true } if every change should not create a history entry.)

valid_evidence.summary: Select 'lamps', refresh: 'lamps' is still selected; press Back: the previous filter returns.
useSearchParams' setter navigates, pushing a history entry unless replace is set.

hints.text: Check where the filter's value is read from on first render.
Step 2 relies on the URL being the only source of the filter.
State kept in the URL survives reloads, can be shared, and participates in history.
Try refresh, copy-link and Back in turn.
This solution is correct. The URL is the single source of truth, so refresh, sharing and Back all work. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: State that describes what the user is looking at - filters, tabs, pages, search terms - often belongs in the URL. Unlike in-memory state, it survives reloads and can be bookmarked and shared.
